_README: Golden evaluation set for the Research Paper RAG system.
IMPORTANT: the 'reference' fields below were drafted from corpus_stats.json and
paper titles. You are the author — review and correct every reference before
trusting the scores. Wrong references produce wrong context_precision and
context_recall numbers. Set 'verified': true once you've checked an item.
id            stable identifier, used as the key in results files
query         the question sent to the RAG system
expected_type one of stats | listing | metadata | content
(also acts as a regression test on classify_query)
reference     ground-truth answer; required by context_precision / context_recall
must_contain  substrings the answer must include (exact track only)
verified      whether you have checked the reference by hand
reference_v1  the earlier single-statement reference, kept for comparison (Oct 13, 2026)

questions.query: How many papers are in this corpus?
questions.reference: The corpus contains 15 papers.
questions.notes: KI-1 (corpus duplication) is fixed: work_id-based dedup at ingestion and retrieval now correctly merges the PDF and metadata representations of the same paper. 15 is the true unique-paper count, confirmed against corpus_stats.json and the author's Google Scholar profile.

questions.reference: The earliest papers date from 2003.

questions.query: What year range does this research span?
questions.reference: The corpus spans 2003 through 2015.

questions.query: What is the total word count across all papers?
questions.reference: The corpus contains 26,890 words in total.
questions.notes: Word count corrected after the KI-1 fix: the old 51,234 double-counted every merged paper's PDF word count plus its short metadata-blob word count.

questions.query: What is the most recent paper in the collection?
questions.reference: The most recent work is the 2015 paper on user modeling of skills and expertise from resumes.

questions.query: List all papers published in 2012.
questions.reference: The 2012 papers are: Discovering Virtual Interest Groups across Chat Rooms; Managing Analysis Context; and Opaque Attribute Alignment.

questions.query: Give me the full list of publications.
questions.reference: The corpus lists 15 papers spanning 2003 to 2015: An Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Search for a Parts Acquisition ePortal (2003); Lessons from the Implementation of an Adaptive Parts Acquisition ePortal (2003); Combating Cognitive Biases in Information Retrieval (2005); Model-Guided Information Discovery for Intelligence Analysis (2005); Profile-Based Security Against Malicious Mobile Agents (2006); Potential IED Threat System (PITS) (2009); Spatial Event Prediction by Combining Value Function Approximation and Case-Based Reasoning (2009); Incremental User Modeling with Heterogeneous User Behaviors (2010); Discovering Virtual Interest Groups across Chat Rooms (2012); Managing Analysis Context (2012); Opaque Attribute Alignment (2012); Discovery of Player Strategies in a Serious Game (2013); Adaptive Interest Modeling Improves Content Services at the Network Edge (2014); User Modeling for Contextual Suggestion (2014); and User Modeling of Skills and Expertise from Resumes (2015).
questions.notes: Updated after the KI-1 fix (21 index entries -> 15 unique papers). List cross-checked against the author's Google Scholar profile.

questions.query: Which papers were published before 2010?
questions.reference: Papers before 2010 include the 2003 parts acquisition ePortal work (and its companion lessons-learned paper), the 2005 papers on cognitive biases in information retrieval and model-guided information discovery, the 2006 profile-based security paper, and the 2009 papers on the Potential IED Threat System and spatial event prediction.

questions.query: Who wrote 'An Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Search for a Parts Acquisition ePortal'?
questions.reference: The authors are Rafael Alonso, Jeffrey A. Bloom, Hua Li, and Chumki Basu. It appeared at the 9th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2003).

questions.query: What venue published the Opaque Attribute Alignment paper?
questions.reference: Opaque Attribute Alignment was published at the IEEE 28th International Conference on Data Engineering Workshops (ICDEW 2012). It was published in 2012.
questions.reference_v1: Opaque Attribute Alignment appeared at the IEEE 28th International Conference on Data Engineering in 2012.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 2 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Corpus metadata gives the venue as the ICDE Workshops (ICDEW 2012); the previous reference said the main ICDE conference. Check which is correct.

questions.query: Who are the authors of the spatial event prediction paper?
questions.reference: The authors are Hua Li, Hector Munoz-Avila, Diane Bramsen, Chad Hogg, and Rafael Alonso. It appeared at the 8th International Conference on Case-Based Reasoning (ICCBR 2009).

questions.query: Where was 'Adaptive Interest Modeling Improves Content Services at the Network Edge' published?
questions.reference: The paper was published at the IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM). It was published in 2014.
questions.reference_v1: It was published at the IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM) in 2014.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 2 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment.

questions.query: Did Jennifer Sleeman coauthor any of these papers?
questions.reference: Yes. Jennifer Sleeman is a coauthor of Opaque Attribute Alignment (IEEE ICDE, 2012), along with Rafael Alonso, Hua Li, Art Pope, and others.
questions.notes: Exercises the proper-noun keyword-supplement path in _retrieve_deduped.

questions.query: What approach was used for spatial event prediction?
questions.reference: The approach is a hybrid of reinforcement-learning value function approximation and case-based reasoning. It learns from historical spatial event patterns. It retrieves analogous past cases to predict future events in geographic space.
questions.reference_v1: The approach combines value function approximation with case-based reasoning to predict the timing and location of events, fusing geographic and non-geographic data sources.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 3 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Dropped 'predicts timing and location' and 'fuses geographic and non-geographic sources': the stored text of this paper does not say so; the timing/location wording appears in the separate 2009 PITS paper. Restore if the ICCBR paper itself says it.

questions.query: What is the core idea behind opaque attribute alignment?
questions.reference: Opaque Attribute Alignment aligns attributes without relying on their names. It estimates the density of each attribute's data with Kernel Density Estimation. It compares those densities, using cross entropy, to decide which attributes align. A similarity hash lets the method handle non-numeric data.
questions.reference_v1: The insight is that semantically similar attributes tend to have similar data distributions or densities, so distributional comparison — using kernel density estimation — can align attributes even when their names and schemas are opaque.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 4 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment.

questions.query: How are virtual interest groups discovered across chat rooms?
questions.reference: The VIGIR tool monitors multiple concurrent chat rooms in real time. It builds adaptive interest models for chat users. It uses those models to identify virtual interest groups, including members a user does not know. It also recommends relevant chat snippets to users.
questions.reference_v1: The system monitors multiple concurrent chat rooms in real time, builds user interest models from conversational activity using NLP and topic modeling, and clusters users with overlapping interests into virtual interest groups so that relevant information can be recommended across rooms.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 4 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Dropped 'NLP and topic modeling' and 'clusters users': the paper lists topics only as future work, and the stored text does not describe clustering.

questions.query: How does the adaptive nearest neighbor search work in the parts acquisition ePortal?
questions.reference: The goal is to find a replacement that is as similar as possible to an obsolete part. Similarity is a weighted distance over part parameters, with larger weights for more important parameters. The Bubble Up algorithm adapts the weights from user feedback when the user selects a part. Iterations continue until the selected part rises higher in the ranked list.
questions.reference_v1: It adapts a nearest-neighbor similarity search to user feedback so that the retrieval of substitute or obsolete parts improves over time, learning which attribute dimensions matter for judging part similarity.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 4 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment.

questions.query: What cognitive biases affect information retrieval according to this research?
questions.reference: The 2005 work presents an anti-bias mechanism (ABM) for combating cognitive biases in information retrieval. ABM automatically generates alternative, competing queries alongside the user's original query. A small set of the best results from the competing queries is mixed in with the original results.
questions.reference_v1: The 2005 work examines how analyst cognitive biases such as confirmation bias distort information seeking and retrieval, and proposes system-side mechanisms to counteract them during search.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 3 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Dropped 'confirmation bias': the 2005 paper's stored text does not name it (it appears in the 2013 serious-game paper).

questions.query: How does adaptive interest modeling improve content services at the network edge?
questions.reference: Adaptive Interest Modeling (AIM) builds a model of each mobile user's interests at the network layer. The interest model drives content prefetching based on recognizing user situations. Users share interest models to stay up to date with each other. Prefetching reduces response time and increases data availability, at the cost of more network bandwidth.
questions.reference_v1: An adaptive model of each mobile user's interests drives content prefetching and peer-to-peer sharing at the network edge, reducing response time and increasing data availability in bandwidth-constrained mobile ad hoc networks.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 4 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Replaced 'peer-to-peer sharing' with interest-model sharing, which is what the paper describes.

questions.query: What method is used to extract skills and expertise from resumes?
questions.reference: The method is called expertise modeling. It takes a resume as input. It produces a quantitative assessment of the competence, or level of mastery, of each skill. It also assesses expertise in each skill domain.
questions.reference_v1: The work presents an algorithm that takes a resume as input and produces an expertise model expressing both the types of skills present and the level of competency in each, rather than treating skills as a flat keyword list.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 4 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Dropped 'rather than treating skills as a flat keyword list': not stated in the stored text.

questions.query: How does incremental user modeling handle heterogeneous user behaviors?
questions.reference: The approach learns user interests incrementally from multiple types of user behaviors or events. Concepts and their relations extracted from these events form the structural elements of the user interest model.
questions.reference_v1: The approach updates a user interest model incrementally as different behavior types arrive, combining heterogeneous signals into a single evolving interest representation rather than requiring batch retraining.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 2 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Dropped 'rather than requiring batch retraining': not stated in the stored text. Two claims only; add one if the paper gives another key step.

questions.query: What security threat does profile-based security address?
questions.reference: It addresses malicious mobile agents in distributed computing environments. Behavior profiles of users and agents are built dynamically. Activity that deviates from the profiles is flagged as anomalous and used for adaptive access control.
questions.reference_v1: It addresses malicious mobile agents by building behavioral profiles of agent activity and detecting agents whose behavior deviates from the expected profile.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 3 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment.

questions.query: What role does context play in managing analysis?
questions.reference: The work detects context switches when an analyst works on multiple tasks at once. It separates contexts with an algorithm based on user modeling. Context switches were detected with 73 percent precision and 70 percent recall at a window of 30 analysis log events.
questions.reference_v1: The Managing Analysis Context work treats an analyst's working context as a first-class object that can be captured, maintained, and used to prioritize and recommend information relevant to the current investigative task.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 3 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Rewritten: the previous reference (prioritizing and recommending information) does not match the stored text, which is about detecting and separating analysis contexts.

questions.query: What is the common thread connecting the user modeling papers across the corpus?
questions.reference: Across the corpus, user interest models are built from observed user behavior. These models drive recommendation, such as virtual interest groups in chat. They drive content prefetching in mobile networks. They drive expertise assessment from resumes.
questions.reference_v1: Across the corpus, user modeling recurs as the mechanism for personalization: interest models are built from observed behavior and then used to drive recommendation, retrieval prioritization, content prefetching, collaboration discovery, and expertise assessment across domains ranging from e-procurement to intelligence analysis to mobile networks.
questions.notes: Oct 13, 2026: split into 4 claims so context recall is not a single yes/no judgment. Kept to four claims, each tied to a paper in the corpus. Swap any for retrieval prioritization or e-procurement if preferred. Earlier note: Cross-paper synthesis — stresses the per-paper deduplication cap.

questions.query: What do these papers say about transformer architectures and attention mechanisms?
questions.reference: The corpus does not cover transformer architectures. The papers span 2003 to 2015 and predate the transformer, so no grounded answer is available from these sources.
